finding: §5.3.2 accepts `--patch` and `--target` as independent inputs and never checks that the mutation actually touches the target. The only constraint on the patch anywhere is §5.3.4 rung 1 — it must apply cleanly — and §5.5's `target` row is validated only as §6.2.3 validates a citation: the path exists and the line is in range. §6.2.2 then requires `target` to fall inside the record's `anchor.start_line`..`anchor.line`, so the entire chain from experiment to assertion runs through one agent-typed flag. A patch that mutates a different file, a comment, or a line of dead code, paired with a `--target` inside the anchor, yields `no-test-failed` and grades the record `probed` — the one register that asserts outright, per §6.2 and §8.1.7 — on an experiment that never touched the cited location. §6.2.2's anchor binding actively creates pressure toward the mismatch: when the real mutation sits outside the anchor, naming an in-anchor target is the only way to get the grade at all, so the rule converts a mismatch into a misreport instead of a rejection. This is the same forgery §6.2.5 closed for `cited` by matching path and line rather than rule id, left open on the stronger grade.
suggestion: Derive the binding from the patch rather than trusting the flag. `cr` holds the unified diff, so require the mutation to modify at least one line in `target`'s file inside `target`'s hunk and reject with exit code 1 naming the probe when it does not — or drop `--target` for `--kind mutation` entirely and compute it from the patch's modified lines. State that gap probes are exempt, since §5.4's supplied test file is new by construction and its binding to the finding is §5.4.4's condition. Add the mutated `path:line` set to the §5.5 probe record and render it in the §8.1.7 evidence region, so the author can check what was broken rather than take it on trust.

finding: §4.1.2 requires an unmapped-unit item for every unit mapped to zero claims and §4.1.5 requires `cr` to attach the issue key's notes to every unmapped unit so the agent can decide whether a note explains it — but no pass of §4.6 can deliver that. §4.6.5's first pass emits the intent prompts with "the units and the claims but no mapping", so at emission time `cr` does not know which units are unmapped and cannot attach notes per §4.1.5 or ask for the item of §4.1.2; the mapping only exists after `cr map record`. §4.6.5 then describes the second invocation as covering "the remaining axes", which reads as excluding intent, so no prompt ever carries the unmapped-unit set. Since §4.6.3 forbids `cr review` from writing findings and §2.1.3 keeps the note judgement with the agent, the item has no producer at all: I cannot decide which command emits it, which role and axis stamp it (both required by §6.1), or where the §4.1.5 note attachment lands.
suggestion: Make the intent axis explicitly two-stage: after `cr map record` succeeds, `cr review <pr> --axis intent` MUST re-emit one prompt per unmapped unit carrying that unit's hunks and the issue key's notes, and that prompt is where the §4.1.2 item and the §4.1.5 note decision are produced. Name the role (`intent-coverage`) and axis (`intent`) the resulting record carries, and say whether the second-pass emission for the other axes may run concurrently with it.

finding: §5.1.6's cleanliness check requires that no file exists under the path `tests.probe_path_template` yields for any probe id. The template yields a path only when given a concrete probe id, and there is no enumerable domain of probe ids: a probe killed mid-run leaves no id in `probes.ndjson` (records are written after the run, and §5.5.1 makes them immutable once written), which is precisely the crash case §5.1.6 and §5.3.3 exist to catch. One engineer wildcards the id position of the resolved template and globs; another iterates the recorded probe ids. Only the first detects the leftover artefact, so the two implementations disagree on the check that §5.1.7 and the revert guarantee rest on.
suggestion: State the scan as a glob: require `tests.probe_path_template` to contain `<probe-id>` exactly once, replace that position with `*` in the resolved template, and treat any filesystem match as a leftover artefact regardless of whether a probe record names it.

finding: §5.2.1 derives `tests_run` and `tests_failed` from `tests.count_pattern` but never says which match is used when the pattern matches the output more than once, nor what happens when a capture group is not a base-10 integer. Test runners routinely print a per-file or per-suite line and a final total that both match the same count regex. A first-match implementation and a last-match implementation then record different counts for the same run, which selects different rungs of §5.3.4 and §5.4.3 — rung 4 (count known and equals zero) versus rung 6 or 5 — and therefore different probe results and different grades. This decides whether a probe can support `probed` at all.
suggestion: Require the last match in the captured output to be used, and require both capture groups to parse as base-10 non-negative integers; a match whose groups do not parse leaves both counts undetermined, exactly as a non-matching pattern does.

finding: Rung 2 of §5.4.3 fires when the runner could not be started, or the supplied test failed to compile or load. The first clause is mechanically observable (exec failure); the second is not — nothing states what output, exit code, or signal constitutes failed to compile or load, and §2.1 forbids `cr` from making that determination. Runners that report a fatal load error as an ordinary failing test produce derivable counts with a non-zero failed count, so a literal implementation falls through to rung 6 and records `failed`, which §5.4.4 escalates to severity at least `high` as evidence the behaviour is wrong — on a test that never executed. An engineer who instead scans `output_tail` for loader errors records `error`, which supports nothing. The ladder declared total over every run therefore has a rung whose predicate cannot be evaluated deterministically, and the disagreement changes the register of a posted comment.
suggestion: Drop the compile/load clause so rung 2 covers only mechanically observable runner-start failure and let rungs 4-6 classify the rest; or define the signal exactly, e.g. an optional per-profile `tests.load_error_pattern` matched against `output_tail`, absent by default.

finding: §6.2.1 defines inside-a-unit as "`path` is one of that unit's file paths and `line` falls within one of its hunk ranges **on the same side**", and §6.2.2 requires a probe's `target` to fall in the anchor range "on the same path and side". Neither value carries a side: §6.1's citation object is `{path, line, content_hash, origin}` and §5.5's `target` is a bare `path:line` validated the way §6.2.3 validates a citation, i.e. resolved against the current head. The side comparison both rules mandate is therefore not computable and I would have to invent one. Assuming RIGHT (the only thing a head resolution can mean) makes the containment guard vacuous for exactly the units §3.4.4 partitions onto the LEFT side: a deletion-only unit's hunk ranges are LEFT line numbers, so no citation can ever be inside it, and every citation — including one the agent aimed at its own unit — grades the record `cited`. That is the self-citation forgery §6.2.1 exists to block, reachable on any PR that deletes code.
suggestion: Add `side` to the citation object in §6.1 as an agent-supplied, validated field (`RIGHT` resolved against the head, `LEFT` against the merge base, mirroring §6.1.2), and to `--target` in §5.3.2/§5.4.2 as `path:side:line` or a separate `--target-side` defaulting to RIGHT. Then state in §6.2.1 that a citation whose side differs from the unit's side is treated as **inside** (not outside) for grading purposes, so a mismatch can never buy the `cited` register.

finding: §6.2.2 admits a `probed` grade only when the probe's `target` falls within the record's `anchor.start_line`..`anchor.line` range on the same path and side, but §5.5's `target` is a bare `path:line` carrying no side and `--target` takes no side argument. One engineer treats every target as `RIGHT` — so no `LEFT`-anchored record can ever be graded `probed` — while another drops the side comparison as unevaluable, under which a probe targeting head line 42 grades a `LEFT`-anchored record covering merge-base line 42, a different piece of code entirely. The predicate is the gate on the only grade permitted to assert, so the two implementations differ on whether an assertion reaches the author.
suggestion: State that a probe target is always `side: RIGHT` because probes run against the sandbox at head, and that a record with a `LEFT` anchor can therefore never be graded `probed`; or extend `--target` to carry a side and validate it against the corresponding tree as §6.2.3 validates a citation.

finding: §8.1.6 discloses two kinds of weak provenance — a machine-generated suggestion (`suggestion_origin: rule`) and a claim resting on a note — and omits the third, which is the one that buys the assert register. Under §6.2 a citation with `origin: rule` grades a record `cited` without the "lies outside the record's own unit" requirement every agent citation must meet, so a regex hit on a changed line plus an agent confirmation that §2.6.1.5 admits `cr` cannot verify is sufficient to post `kind: finding`. The author then receives an assertion whose §8.1.7 evidence region lists a `path:line` inside their own diff, with nothing saying that location came from a pattern match. The asymmetry is exact: the machine-generated fix is disclosed, the machine-generated evidence is not. §2.6.4's "MUST be able to quote the rule's `rationale`" is a capability rather than an obligation, and the record's `rule` field is never rendered anywhere, so the standard the author is being held to may never reach them either.
suggestion: Extend §8.1.6's trigger set to a record whose grade rests on a citation with `origin: rule`, and have the generated region name the rule id and quote its `rationale`, so the disclosure and the standard arrive together. Alternatively upgrade §2.6.4 from "MUST be able to quote" to "MUST quote" and route it through the `cr`-owned provenance region of §8.1.3, so a convention comment can never reach the author as a bare assertion about a line.

finding: §4.5.4 forbids `cr` from reporting a round complete without stating which axes did not run, and §11.1 forbids `--quiet` from suppressing that disclosure — but both obligations stop at the reviewer's terminal. The only surface `cr` owns in the artefact the author actually reads is the review body of §8.4.3, and the spec puts nothing in it but an HTML comment holding the payload hash. A review posted with the intent axis unavailable per §4.5.3, the test axis disabled per §4.5.2, units flagged `oversized` per §3.4.5, or cells still unfilled therefore arrives as a set of line comments and an empty body. Absence of a comment reads as "I looked and found nothing", which is the cheapest overstatement of certainty available, and §8.4.3 already establishes that the review body is not a line comment and is unaffected by §1.6.1, so the room exists at no comment-economy cost. §10.2's own sentence — completeness across three axes is not completeness across four — is addressed to the wrong reader.
suggestion: Require the review body to carry, above the payload-hash comment of §8.4.3, the disclosure §4.5.4 already computes: the active axes, the disabled and unavailable ones with their reasons, and whether the coverage matrix had gaps. Make it a `cr`-owned generated region on the same terms as §8.1.3's, not editable and not composable by the agent, and state explicitly that it is exempt from `post.max_comments` because it is not a line comment.

finding: §9.3.2 names exactly three verbs to refuse at a moved head — draft, post, probe. `cr record`, `cr merge`, `cr map record`, `cr cells record` and `cr claims record` all write per-PR state keyed by round and head, and none is listed; §9.3.1 requires only that the divergence be reported. A tester cannot decide what `cr record` does after a force-push: exit 4 like the other write paths, or exit 0 and admit records carrying the new head into a round whose units, claims, and mapping were computed at the old one, leaving §10.2.2's unit-hash check as the only downstream guard.
suggestion: Either extend §9.3.2's refusal to every command that writes per-PR state, naming `cr brief` as the only way to move forward, or state explicitly that those commands proceed and that each incoming record's `head` is validated against `meta.json`'s recorded head, with a mismatch rejected at exit code 4.

finding: §9.3.4 says `cr brief` MUST "recompute units, threads, and the claim set for the new head", but §3.3.3 says `cr` MUST NOT re-extract claims and that re-extraction happens only through a new `cr claims record`, and claims carry a required `head` (§3.3) plus `round` (§2.3.3) while §9.3.5 restricts every command to the current round's records. There is no operation `cr` can perform to "recompute the claim set": it cannot re-derive claims (invariant 1) and it cannot restamp the old ones without doing exactly the replace that §3.3.1 reserves for `cr claims record`. Implemented literally, the first round after a head change has zero current-round claims, so §4.1.1-§4.1.3 raise nothing, §4.1.7 derives an empty `intent-gaps.ndjson`, and §10.2.3 passes vacuously — the intent axis silently evaporates on every push while still being reported active. Nothing requires the agent to re-run `cr claims record` either.
suggestion: Replace "the claim set" in §9.3.4 with the two things `cr` can actually do: re-read the issue text and re-run the §3.3.3 drift comparison, and carry each prior claim forward into the new round unchanged except for restamped `head`/`round`, recording that the carry-forward happened. State explicitly that a carried-forward claim keeps its `span_hash`/`issue_hash` from extraction time so drift stays detectable, and that `cr map record` is required again because §9.3.4 cleared the mapping.

finding: §10.3 has three commands "accumulate their own counts into `rounds/<n>/summary.json`", and §6.5.1 has `cr merge` "write its drop counts" there. Accumulation is additive, and none of these commands is once-per-round: §7.1.6 explicitly contemplates regenerating the draft, §8.5.1 makes a `cr post` dry run the normal precursor to `cr post --confirm`, and re-running `cr merge` after fixing one role's output file is the obvious recovery path. Each re-run inflates the waived, deduplicated, and drafted counts. §7.3.1 identified this exact hazard for triage events and solved it by keying on `(PR, round, record id, action)` and overwriting; §10.3 carries no equivalent rule, so the round summary — the artefact §10.3 says makes "the history of a review reconstructable from state alone" — is the one place where re-running a command silently changes the record.
suggestion: Give §10.3 the §7.3.1 treatment: each writing command MUST replace its own section of `summary.json` on every invocation rather than add to it, so the file is a function of current state and re-running a command is idempotent. State which keys belong to which writer, mirroring §10.3's new writer list.

finding: §10.3 now names the writers of `summary.json` — "`cr merge`, `cr draft`, and `cr post` MUST each accumulate their own counts" — but two of the counts it mandates arise at a command that is not on that list. `cr record` is what stamps `duplicate` from `duplicate_of` (§6.4.3, §9.1) and what writes state `suppressed` for a finding an existing human thread already covers (§3.5.4, §9.1's `draft` → `suppressed` row). `cr merge` emits `duplicate_of` but never stamps state, and `cr draft` and `cr post` see only queued records. So the "deduplicated" and "suppressed by thread" counts have no named producer, and the closed writer list makes that a hole rather than an unstated liberty.
suggestion: Add `cr record` to §10.3's writer list and assign it the deduplicated and thread-suppressed counts, or state that `cr draft` derives both by counting the current round's records in states `duplicate` and `suppressed` before it queues. Either way, name a writer for every count §10.3 lists.

finding: §9.3.6 requires a finding dropped by the posted index to be counted in the round summary, but §10.3's enumeration of the counts every round must record has no entry for it: raised, deduplicated, suppressed by thread, waived, forced to question, drafted, posted, discarded as not-here, discarded as wrong. One engineer folds posted-index drops into `waived` (the two are described as behaving identically), another adds a distinct key. A test asserting the shape of `summary.json`, or asserting that a re-raised posted finding is visibly accounted for, cannot be written.
suggestion: Add an explicit already-posted drop count per §9.3.6 to §10.3's list, kept separate from `waived` so the two suppression reasons stay distinguishable in the reconstructable history §10.3 promises.

finding: §2.3.3 requires every record in `claims.ndjson`, `mapping.ndjson`, `coverage.ndjson` (among others) to carry `head` and `round`, but none of the three schemas agrees. §3.3's claim table has `head` as agent-required and no `round` row at all; §4.1.6 defines a mapping line as just `{claim, unit}`; §4.5.5 lists the fields a cell must carry, including "the head it was filled against", and never mentions `round`. Meanwhile §6.1 makes `head` and `round` agent-written required fields on findings and does *not* mark them computed, so across the four agent-input commands it is undecidable whether the agent supplies these fields or `cr` stamps them — and nothing says what happens when an agent supplies a `round` other than the current one, which under §9.3.5 would write a record no command ever reads again.
suggestion: State once, in §2.3.3, that `head` and `round` are stamped by `cr` on write for every file listed there and MUST NOT be supplied by the agent, then mark them `computed` in §3.3, §4.5.5, and §6.1 so §6.1.4's rejection rule covers them uniformly. Drop `head` from §3.3's agent-required rows accordingly.

finding: `tests.probe_path_template` is typed only as `string`, and its default is written in prose as `<root of the first tests.globs entry>/cr_probe_<probe-id><ext>`. Nothing defines the template's substitution vocabulary: whether `<probe-id>` and `<ext>` are literal placeholder tokens (§3.1 uses a different syntax, `{key}`), what other placeholders are legal, or where `<ext>` comes from — a gap probe's file arrives through `--test <file>` (§5.4.2), a mutation probe has no file at all, and profiles are supposed to set the template themselves. §5.1.6 compounds it by requiring `cr` to check that "no file under the path `tests.probe_path_template` yields for any probe id" exists; probe ids are unbounded, so this is only checkable by turning the template into a glob, which needs the placeholder token to be identifiable. I would have to invent all three rules.
suggestion: Define the template as a string over an enumerated placeholder set — exactly `{probe_id}` and `{ext}` — state that `{ext}` is the extension of the file supplied to `--test` (and that a mutation probe never expands the template), require `{probe_id}` to appear at least once, and define §5.1.6's leftover check as the template with `{probe_id}` replaced by `*` and `{ext}` by `.*`, matched as a glob.

finding: `tests.probe_path_template`'s default is given as `<root of the first tests.globs entry>/cr_probe_<probe-id><ext>`. `<root>` is defined exactly (longest leading path prefix free of `*`, `?`, `[`) and `<probe-id>` is defined by §5.5, but `<ext>` is defined nowhere. Three readings give different paths: the extension implied by the first `tests.globs` entry (`tests/**/*.php` yields `.php`), the extension of the file the agent passed to `--test`, or a per-profile constant. Only the first is available to §5.1.6's cleanliness scan, which must resolve the template with no supplied file, so a placement test and a leftover-detection test can be written against different paths for the same profile.
suggestion: Define `<ext>` mechanically from the first `tests.globs` entry — the literal suffix following the last wildcard segment — and require it to be resolvable without a supplied test file, aborting with exit code 3 naming the profile when it is not.

finding: §2.6.3.4 requires `cr rules list --dead --repo <owner/repo>` to report rules with no hit and no record "across the last `rules.dead_after` rounds", but round indices are per-PR (§2.3 `meta.json`, §9.3.3), so "the last 20 rounds" has no repository-wide meaning: PR 7 round 3 and PR 12 round 3 are different rounds with the same index. §2.6.1.6 fixes the `rule-stats.ndjson` entry as rule id, path, line, round, and head — no PR identifier and no timestamp — so the entries cannot even be grouped by PR, let alone ordered across PRs. The same file is the positional authority for §6.2.5's `origin: rule` stamping, which works only because it matches on head; dead-rule detection has no such anchor. As written the command is not implementable.
suggestion: Add `pr` and a UTC timestamp to the `rule-stats.ndjson` entry in §2.6.1.6, and redefine §2.6.3.4's window as the last `rules.dead_after` distinct `(pr, round)` pairs ordered by timestamp descending, stating that a rule counts as alive if it produced a hit or a record in any of them.

finding: §3.4.6 assigns unit ids "in ascending order of first file path then first changed line", but §3.4.4 partitions a file's hunks by side and states that adjacency, the §3.4.5 split, and the §3.4.6 hash order "compare line numbers only within one side". The id ordering is the one comparison that must range over both sides at once, and a file that contains both a RIGHT-sided unit and a LEFT-sided unit can produce two units whose first changed line is the same number in two different coordinate spaces. The ordering is then not total, id assignment is undetermined, and §2.1.1's reproducibility requirement is unmet — two conforming implementations will number the same diff differently.
suggestion: Add a side tiebreak to §3.4.6: order by first file path ascending, then side (`LEFT` before `RIGHT`, matching §8.3.3's existing convention), then first changed line ascending. State that this is the one place where a cross-side comparison is defined, so it does not read as contradicting §3.4.4.

finding: §2.3 lists `meta.json`, `units.ndjson`, and `threads.ndjson` as per-PR state that later sections read as authoritative — §4.5.6 and §4.1.6 reject unknown unit ids, §9.3.1/§9.3.3 read and write `meta.json`'s recorded head and round index, §3.5.3 attaches ingested threads — yet no command is required to create any of them. §3.7 says `cr brief` "MAY compute and persist the derived inputs of §3.3 through §3.6", and the only MUST is the conditional one in §9.3.4 that fires on a head change. On a first-ever run at an unchanged head, nothing obliges these three files to exist, and no section says what round index a fresh `meta.json` starts at or which command creates it. I would have to decide whether `cr review`, `cr cells record`, and `cr map record` recompute units on the fly or fail.
suggestion: Turn the §3.7 permission into an obligation: `cr brief` MUST create `meta.json` (round index starting at 1, recorded head set to the current head) and MUST persist `units.ndjson` and `threads.ndjson` for the current round. Add a sentence saying every other command that reads them MUST fail with exit code 4 and a hint naming `cr brief` when they are absent, rather than recomputing.

finding: §4.4.2 obliges the agent to enumerate up to `test.max_edge_cases` expected edge cases for every claim and mark each asserted, missing, or not applicable with a reason, and obliges `cr` to report the cap when it binds — but no file in §2.2 or §2.3 holds the enumeration, no field in §4.5.5 or §6.1 carries it, no later rule consumes it, and it changes no grade. Meanwhile §4.6.1 fans out per `(role, unit)`, so a claim mapped to several units has its enumeration regenerated once per unit with no dedup rule and no shared store. What the spend buys is at best an `argued` finding, which §4.4.4 routes to the question channel regardless of how thorough the enumeration was. This is recall paid for in tokens and wall-clock at every unit, with no reduction in the chance of a wrong assertion — and a cap-reporting obligation on a list that has no reader.
suggestion: Either give the enumeration a home and a consumer — record it once per claim keyed by claim id, and make a `missing` entry the specific input that §4.4.3 escalates to a gap probe, so the spend converts into `probed` evidence — or demote it from a MUST on the agent to guidance inside the `test-adequacy` role's `instructions`, where a role-owned heuristic belongs, and drop the cap and its reporting obligation with it.

finding: §4.5.5 requires every cell to carry "the head it was filled against, the unit hash of §3.4.6 it was filled for", and §4.5.6 makes cells agent-supplied through `cr cells record`, which is only required to reject an unknown unit id or an inactive role. Neither field is marked computed the way §6.1's schema marks `grade`, so the agent writes both. §10.2.2 then rests completeness on "every one of those cells was filled for that unit's current unit hash" — a guard whose input is the very thing being guarded. An agent that echoes the current hash makes a stale cell indistinguishable from a fresh one, and P6's "coverage is proven" reduces to coverage asserted.
suggestion: Mark `head` and the unit hash as computed on the cell: `cr cells record` stamps both from the current head and from `units.ndjson` for the named unit id, and rejects with exit code 1 a cell that arrives carrying either — the same treatment §6.1.4 gives `grade`. Then §10.2.2's check is a comparison against state `cr` owns, and a cell recorded before a re-cluster fails it automatically.

finding: §4.5.6 accepts a cell's value — `pass`, `finding`, `question`, `na` — as agent judgement and cross-checks nothing beyond the unit id and whether the role is active, yet §10.1.1 and §10.2.2 report the resulting matrix as the proof that the diff was examined, and P6 calls coverage proven. A role can file a `pass` cell for a unit while recording a finding on that same unit in the same round, and `cr status` will print a complete row and a clean verdict. One direction of this admits no legitimate exception: a `pass` cell cannot coexist with a surviving record from the same role on the same unit, because a waiver drop (§6.4.4) and a posted-index drop (§9.3.6) can only remove records, never create them.
suggestion: Require `cr cells record` to reject with exit code 1, or `cr status` to report, any `(unit, role)` carrying a `pass` cell for which the current round holds a record from that role on that unit, naming both. Leave the opposite direction unenforced and say why — a `finding` cell with no surviving record is the expected outcome of §6.4.4 and §9.3.6 — so the asymmetry reads as deliberate rather than as an omission.

finding: §5.5 now defines `baseline` per kind — for `gap` it is the unfiltered run, "since the probe's own test does not exist in the baseline" — but §5.2.2 was not updated alongside it and still says "A filtered probe MUST additionally record a filtered baseline for the same filter on unmutated code." A gap probe is a filtered probe (§5.4.2 takes `--filter`), so §5.2.2 mandates a run whose filter selects a file that does not yet exist: `tests_run` is 0, so §5.2.5 makes it `passed: false` permanently, and no rule anywhere consumes it. Worse, an implementer who reads §5.2.2 as authoritative will wire that run in as the gap probe's baseline and re-open exactly the unreachable-`probed` defect §5.5 was changed to close. The phrase "on unmutated code" also reads as mutation-only, leaving it genuinely unclear whether the sentence binds gap probes at all.
suggestion: Scope §5.2.2's second sentence to mutation probes: "A mutation probe run with a filter MUST additionally record a filtered baseline for the same filter on unmutated code. A gap probe's baseline is the unfiltered run per §5.5." Cross-reference §5.5's per-kind table so the two sections cannot drift again.

finding: §5.4.4 and §5.4.5 bound a gap finding's severity by what the probe established — at least `high` only when the probe supports the finding, at most `medium` when the probe merely passed — but `severity` is an agent-written required field under §6.1, is not marked computed, and §6.1.3's validation checks presence alone. No command is named as the enforcer, so both MUSTs bind nobody, unlike the grade, which §6.2.1 pins to `cr` and §7.2.2 recomputes at post time. Every input is available to `cr`: the probe id, its kind, its result, its baseline, and whether it supports the record under §6.2.2. The cost is not a wrong assertion but a misdirected human — severity is what the reviewer triages on under the blocking cap of §1.6.2, so a probe that proved only a missing test can present its finding as the loudest item in the draft.
suggestion: Name the enforcer. State that `cr record` MUST reject with exit code 1 a gap-probe-backed record whose severity violates §5.4.4 or §5.4.5, naming the record, the probe, and the result, and that `cr post` MUST re-check the bound after triage the way §7.2.2 re-checks the grade. If a reviewer's hand-raised severity is instead meant to survive triage under §7.2's "freely editable" row, say so explicitly and confine the bound to record time, so the two rules stop contradicting each other silently.

finding: `citations[].content_hash` is marked computed and is the one hash in the document with no stated pre-image. §1.4 fixes the transformation, and §3.4.6, §7.4.1, §8.3.3 and §9.2 each name exactly what is hashed; §6.2.3 says only that `cr` computes and stores it at record time. Whether it covers the single line at `path:line`, that line plus the §9.2 context window, or the whole cited file is undetermined, so two implementations produce values that cannot be compared — which is exactly the comparability §6.2.3 says a v0.2 drift check will depend on. No assertion about a stored citation can be written today.
suggestion: Define it as the normalised hash per §1.4 of the single line at `path:line` resolved on the side the citation was validated against, matching §9.2's rule for a one-line anchor.

finding: §6.2.1's inside/outside predicate ("`line` falls within one of its hunk ranges **on the same side**") and §6.2.2's probe-support predicate ("falls within that record's `anchor.start_line`..`anchor.line` range on the same path **and side**") both compare a side that neither operand carries. A citation is `{path, line, content_hash, origin}` per §6.1 and a probe `target` is a bare `path:line` per §5.5 — no `side` field exists on either. Since §6.2.3 resolves citations against the current head and §5.5 validates `target` the same way, both are implicitly RIGHT, which has a consequence the spec never states: §3.4.1/§3.4.4 admit LEFT-sided units for deletion-only hunks, so for such a unit no probe target can ever fall on the same side and a deletion finding can never reach `probed`, while every citation is automatically "outside the record's own unit" and therefore buys `cited` for free.
suggestion: Either add `side` to the `citations` entry and to the probe `target` (defaulting to `RIGHT`, validated against the merge base when `LEFT`), or state explicitly in §6.2.1/§6.2.2 that citations and probe targets are RIGHT-side only and say what that means for a LEFT-anchored record — that it cannot be graded `probed`, and that the inside/outside test does not apply to it.

finding: The dedup key of §6.4.1 is `(anchor.path, anchor.line, class)` and omits `anchor.side`, although §9.2 makes side part of an anchor and §6.1.2 resolves the two sides against different trees. A record about a removed line at merge-base line 40 and a record about an added line at head line 40 in the same file with the same class collapse into one duplicate group, and §6.4.3 retires one of them in state `duplicate`. §7.4.1's waiver key also omits side but is protected by the anchored-line content hash, and §3.4.4 was just tightened so that a unit never mixes sides; §6.4.1 is the remaining place where the two coordinate spaces are compared as if they were one.
suggestion: Include `anchor.side` in the §6.4.1 dedup key, and reflect it where §7.4.1 says its key matches the class-based identity of §6.4.1.

finding: §9.3.6 says a finding matching the posted index "MUST be dropped at merge", and §6.5.1 makes `cr merge` the sole applier of §6.4.4 and §9.3.6. But nothing requires `cr record`'s input to be `cr merge`'s output: §11 lists `cr record <pr> <file>` with no precondition, §6.1.3 has `cr merge` and `cr record` performing the same required-field validation on the same shape, and the single-role case (one NDJSON file) makes skipping merge the obvious thing to do. A pipeline that skips merge therefore re-raises a finding already posted in an earlier round, which is the exact repeat-assertion the posted index was added to prevent. §7.4.7 hedges this for waivers by also requiring the drop "before drafting", so waivers have two enforcement points and the posted index has one.
suggestion: Either require `cr record` to reject input that is not `cr merge` output (e.g. a merge-stamped header line or a required provenance field), or move the §6.4.4 and §9.3.6 drops so that `cr record` MUST re-apply them idempotently before writing anything to `findings.ndjson`. Pick one and say so in both §6.5.1 and §9.3.6, since the invariant is that a posted finding never reaches a second draft, not that a particular command ran.

finding: §7.1.1 requires each block to be introduced by an HTML comment marker carrying `id`, `kind`, `path`, `start_line`, `line`, `severity`, `grade`, and `disposition`, but never gives its syntax, while §7.2 defines per-field edit semantics, §7.2.1 aborts when a marker is malformed, §7.2.3 aborts on an unknown id, and §8.1.3 rejects both a body containing the marker comment and a body containing any `<!-- cr:` sequence. Whether those last two are one rule or two depends on whether the marker shares the `cr:` prefix of §8.1.3's newly named region delimiters. The entire triage input channel is parsed from a grammar the spec never fixes, so no malformed-marker or marker-edit test can be written, and no test can decide which exit path a body carrying a marker-like string takes.
suggestion: Give the marker's exact syntax with one example line, state whether it uses the `<!-- cr:` prefix reserved by §8.1.3, and define malformed as any deviation from that grammar.

finding: §7.1.6 preserves bodies for records whose body differs from `rendered.json` without saying whether the comparison is byte-exact against the stored region or normalised per §1.4, while §7.1.5 stores each region exactly as rendered and, separately, a normalised hash of all regions concatenated in marker order, calling that hash the only observable basis for detecting a user edit. A hash over the concatenation cannot identify which record changed, so it cannot be the basis §7.1.6 uses; and the two available comparisons disagree on whether a whitespace-only or line-ending-only edit preserves the human's body or lets regeneration overwrite it.
suggestion: State that edit detection is a byte-exact comparison of each record's stored agent region against the current draft's corresponding region, and either drop the concatenated hash or describe it as a whole-file integrity marker that plays no part in per-record preservation.

finding: §7.2's marker table says a `severity` edit is freely editable and recorded as a triage event, but §7.3.1 closes the action vocabulary at five names (raised, kept, softened, discarded-not-here, discarded-wrong), allows `cr post --confirm` exactly one outcome event per queued record, and enumerates the fields an event carries without `severity`. A record whose only draft edit is a severity change therefore requires an event that cannot be named, cannot be added without breaking the exactly-one rule, and could not represent the change if it were written.
suggestion: Either add `severity-changed` to the vocabulary of §7.3.1 and exempt it from the one-outcome-event-per-record rule, or add `severity` to the fields every event carries and state that a severity edit is recorded on the record's single outcome event rather than as an event of its own.

finding: §7.3.1 keys triage events by `(PR, round, record id, action)` and claims this makes counts non-inflatable. It does not, because `action` is part of the key: a record can accumulate two different outcome events for the same round. The reachable path is the ordinary retry after §8.4.2 — `cr post --confirm` MUST write exactly one outcome event per queued record with no stated ordering relative to the network call, GitHub rejects the review so nothing is marked posted and the records stay `queued`, the reviewer then sets `disposition=wrong` on one of them and re-runs. That record now carries both `kept` and `discarded-wrong` against a single `raised`, so §7.3.2's per-class report shows outcomes exceeding raises and §7.3.4's demotion rate is inflated on precisely the class the retry touched.
suggestion: Key outcome events on `(PR, round, record id)` with the action as a value, so a later run replaces the earlier outcome, and keep `raised` as a separate keyed event. Also state whether `cr post --confirm` writes its outcome events before or after the network call, and that a call rejected per §8.4.2 MUST leave no outcome event behind.

finding: §8.1.1 makes comment language `render.lang`, "defaulting to `tr`", with no enumerated domain, while §8.1.4 requires the question label to be "built in per `render.lang`" and explicitly non-configurable — §2.7 even forbids any layer from addressing it. These cannot both hold for a free-form string: for `render.lang: de` there is no built-in label, and §6.3's forcing would reach the reader through nothing. §8.1.5's `?` check is also language-dependent in principle. I cannot ship without knowing the label table's key set and what happens on an unknown value.
suggestion: Enumerate the valid `render.lang` values for v0.1 (`tr` and `en`), state that any other value aborts with exit code 3 naming the setting, and give the built-in label text for each enumerated language in the spec so it is testable rather than an implementation choice.

finding: §10.3 requires every round's `summary.json` to record the payload hash of §8.3.3, but a round that is drafted and never posted, or run only through §8.5.1's dry run, has no posted payload — and §10.3 itself says the file is finalised by `cr post`. Whether the key is absent, null, or holds the hash of the dry-run payload is undetermined, so an assertion over an unposted round's summary cannot be written.
suggestion: Say that the payload hash is recorded only once `cr post --confirm` has built a payload and is absent otherwise, and that an unfinalised summary is a valid terminal state for a round.

finding: `tests.probe_path_template`'s default is given as `<root of the first `tests.globs` entry>/cr_probe_<probe-id><ext>`. The round-7 repair defined the root precisely ("the longest leading path prefix free of `*`, `?`, and `[`") and `<probe-id>` is fixed by §5.5, but `<ext>` is defined nowhere in the document. Nothing says whether it is the extension of the first `tests.globs` entry, a profile-declared value, or the language's conventional test extension. The blast radius is limited because the same row requires each shipped profile to set the template explicitly, so only user-authored profiles hit the default — but §5.1.6's leftover-artefact check and §5.4.2's collision abort both scan the path the template yields, and an implementation that guesses wrong makes both checks miss.
suggestion: Define `<ext>` in the same row, most naturally as "the file extension of the first `tests.globs` entry, or empty when it has none", so the default is computable from data the profile already carries.

finding: Every branch of §3.4.4 clusters within one file — same file and enclosing symbol, same file and adjacency, or one unit per hunk — so a unit always has exactly one file path. §3.4.6 nonetheless stores its file paths and orders the unit-hash pre-image file by file in ascending path order, and §6.2.1 tests whether a path is one of that unit's file paths. No constructible diff exercises the cross-file ordering, so the clause cannot be tested and its correctness is never pinned by the suite.
suggestion: Either state that a unit is single-file and simplify §3.4.6's pre-image and §6.2.1's containment test accordingly, or name the case — a rename pair, for instance — that puts two paths into one unit so the ordering rule becomes reachable.

finding: §4.5.1 defines a role as active when "its axis is active, its `profiles` list is empty or names the resolved profile, and §4.6.4 did not report it skipped", while §4.6.1 has `cr review` emit a prompt "for every active role" and §4.6.4 reports a role skipped when "its prerequisites are unmet". Activeness is thus defined in terms of an output of the command that consumes it, and the "prerequisites" that drive the skip are never enumerated separately from the axis conditions of §4.5.2 and §4.5.3. `cr cells record` (§4.5.6) and completeness (§10.2.2) both need the active set independently of whether `cr review` has run, and §2.3's `meta.json` stores "active roles" without saying which command computes it.
suggestion: State the condition directly — a role is active when its axis is active and its `profiles` list is empty or names the resolved profile — and recast §4.6.4 as the reporting obligation for the negative case rather than as an input to the definition. Name the command that computes and stores `meta.json`'s active-role list.

finding: §5.1.6's **post-setup baseline** is durable cross-process state: it is recorded once at sandbox creation, after §5.1.2 and §5.1.3 complete, and then read "before every probe or test run" by later `cr` invocations. §2.3's per-PR state table has no file for it, and §2.2 places nothing under the sandbox directory but the worktree itself. An implementer has to invent a location, and §2.2's rule that `cr` MUST NOT write inside the repository under review makes the obvious choice — a dotfile in the sandbox — a candidate for violating an invariant, since the sandbox is a worktree of that repository.
suggestion: Add a row to §2.3 such as `sandbox-baseline.json` — the tracked-file state recorded per §5.1.6 — and say it is invalidated whenever the sandbox is recreated. That also settles that the baseline lives outside the worktree, so recording it cannot be mistaken for a write into the repository under review.

finding: §5.2.2 requires that "a filtered probe MUST additionally record a filtered baseline for the same filter on unmutated code", which collides with §5.5's per-kind `baseline` definition: a gap probe's baseline is the unfiltered run "since the probe's own test does not exist in the baseline". For a filtered gap probe the mandated filtered baseline runs a filter that selects only the not-yet-created probe test, so `tests_run` is 0 and §5.2.5 forces `passed: false`. `cr` is required to perform and store a run record that can never pass and that §5.2.6 will never resolve as a baseline.
suggestion: Scope §5.2.2's second sentence to mutation probes: "A filtered **mutation** probe MUST additionally record a filtered baseline for the same filter on unmutated code; a gap probe uses the unfiltered baseline per §5.5 and MUST NOT record a filtered one."

finding: §5.6.4 says `probe.max_per_round` "MUST cap probe executions per round; the cap being hit MUST be reported, never silently applied", but does not say what `cr probe run` does on the run that exceeds it. §1.6.2 sets the pattern for the other cap — block with exit code 1 and name the count — while §5.6.2 uses exit code 4 for the neighbouring lock timeout, so both are defensible and I would have to pick one.
suggestion: State it explicitly: "A `cr probe run` that would exceed `probe.max_per_round` MUST refuse with exit code 1, naming the cap and the count of probes already run in this round, and MUST NOT execute anything in the sandbox."

finding: §6.4.1 dedups on `(anchor.path, anchor.line, class)` and §7.4.1 keys waivers on `(anchor.path, class, normalised hash of the anchored lines)`; neither includes `anchor.side`, although §9.2 makes side part of what an anchor means and §3.4.4 now goes to the trouble of never letting a unit mix sides. A record about a deleted line at LEFT:120 and a record about an added line at RIGHT:120 in the same file with the same class collapse into one duplicate group, and the representative rule of §6.4.2 then silences the other with no observable reason.
suggestion: Add `anchor.side` to the dedup key in §6.4.1 and to the waiver/posted-index key in §7.4.1, and note in §7.4.1 that the added side keeps the key aligned with §9.2's definition of anchor identity.

finding: §7.4.6 says a waiver for a rule-produced record "MAY be widened to a path prefix", but no command widens one: §11 offers only `cr waivers list` and `cr waivers remove`, §7.4.1 fixes the key as `(anchor.path, class, hash)`, §7.4.4 names the two files, and §7.4.8 covers listing and removal only. Nothing defines a prefix-form key, how §6.4.4 matches against it, or who writes it, so the sentence has no implementable content.
suggestion: Either drop §7.4.6 from v0.1, or give it a mechanism: a `--prefix <path>` flag on a `cr waivers add` command, a stated key form (prefix in place of `anchor.path`, with the anchored-lines hash omitted), and a matching rule in §6.4.4 saying a prefix waiver matches any record whose `anchor.path` is under it with the same class.

finding: §9.3.6 says "`cr` MUST maintain a **posted index** in `posted-index.ndjson` ... holding one entry per record that reached `posted`", and §6.5.1 makes `cr merge` a reader of it. No command is named as the writer. The only transition into `posted` is `cr post --confirm` or `cr post --reconcile` on adopt (§9.1), so the answer is inferable, but the file is load-bearing — a missing entry silently re-raises a comment the author already received — and §10.3's new writer list shows the document is otherwise explicit about ownership.
suggestion: Name the writer in §9.3.6: `cr post` appends one entry per record it moves to `posted`, on `--confirm` and on `--reconcile` adopt alike, keyed per §7.4.1.
